strengths: Introduction of a novel, naturalistic, document-level, cross-lingual dataset (SwissGov-RSD) with fine-grained human annotations, filling a significant gap in the literature which has been dominated by synthetic or sentence-level benchmarks.

Comprehensive benchmarking involving a diverse suite of models, including modern encoder models (e.g., ModernBERT, EuroBERT, Qwen3) and large language models (e.g., LLaMA-3.1, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1), evaluated across unsupervised, few-shot, and fine-tuned settings.

Clear, robust, and impactful findings showing a massive performance drop when models transition from synthetic benchmarks to real-world naturalistic datasets, which serves as a realistic reality check for the field.
Highly detailed supplementary material, including thorough annotation guidelines, prompt templates, and a detailed analysis of annotator discrepancy.
weaknesses: The inter-annotator agreement metrics (e.g., Mean F1 of 18.09% for EN-DE and 33.34% for EN-FR) are notably low. While the authors address this and highlight that subjective differences are typical in translation error annotation, the high subjectivity indicates that the gold labels are potentially noisy.

The absolute performance of all evaluated models on the SwissGov-RSD benchmark is very low (Spearman correlation coefficients rarely exceed 25%). This suggests that the current formulations of token-level RSD are extremely challenging and might require alternative evaluation frameworks or model paradigms.

The dataset size is relatively modest (224 document pairs), and it is restricted to high-resource Indo-European languages (German, French, Italian) paired with English, limiting the generalizability of the findings to low-resource languages or different language families.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored task: token-level Recognition of Semantic Differences (RSD) at the document level using natural, cross-lingual data.
Introduces SwissGov-RSD, a high-quality human-annotated dataset of naturally occurring semantic differences between English and three major European languages (German, French, Italian).
Provides a thorough evaluation of diverse architectures, including unsupervised encoder models, few-shot prompted LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1), and fine-tuned models.

The analysis delivers valuable, realistic insights: it highlights the severe limitations of synthetic benchmarks (like iSTS-RSD) and exposes major formatting and length limitations of LLMs when performing structured token-level prediction on long documents.
weaknesses: The inter-annotator agreement is quite low, particularly for the English-German pair (e.g., Mean F1 score of ~18%). While the authors justify this by comparing it to similarly subjective tasks like translation error span annotation, it indicates a high level of noise and subjectivity in the gold standard labels.

The size of the dataset is relatively small (224 document pairs), which limits the ability to perform robust fine-tuning directly on this dataset without relying on synthetic out-of-domain data or label projection.

The language coverage is restricted to high-resource, closely related European languages (German, French, Italian) sharing Latin scripts, meaning the findings may not generalize to typologically distant or non-Latin script languages.

strengths: Introduces SwissGov-RSD, the first naturalistic, human-annotated, document-level, cross-lingual dataset for token-level recognition of semantic differences, filling an important gap in the evaluation of fine-grained text alignment.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation comparing a wide variety of state-of-the-art models, including massive multilingual encoders (like EuroBERT and ModernBERT) and powerful LLMs (like GPT-4o, Llama-3.1, and reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1 and o3-mini).

Provides highly insightful and sobering findings, demonstrating a massive performance gap between synthetic benchmarks and real-world naturalistic datasets, which warns against overestimating model capabilities based on synthetic evaluations.
Well-structured paper with thorough documentation of the annotation process, including detailed guidelines, inter-annotator agreement metrics, and an honest analysis of annotator discrepancy.
weaknesses: The inter-annotator agreement on exact span alignment (measured by IoU) is quite low, particularly for English-German (mean IoU of ~11%), highlighting the high subjectivity of the task, though this is partially mitigated by manual inspection and is common for fine-grained semantic tasks.

The scope of the benchmark is limited to English-centric pairs and high-resource European languages (German, French, Italian) with Latin scripts, leaving typographic and structural variations in more distant languages unexplored.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-studied NLP task: token-level Recognition of Semantic Differences (RSD) at the document level.

Introduces SwissGov-RSD, a highly realistic, multi-parallel, human-annotated dataset featuring naturally occurring discrepancies in official Swiss government documents across English, German, French, and Italian.
The annotation pipeline is rigorous, including fair compensation for student annotators, trial phases, detailed multi-page guidelines, and automatic agreement checks.

Comprehensive and highly up-to-date empirical evaluation covering a wide variety of state-of-the-art encoder models (e.g., EuroBERT, ModernBERT) and large language models (including reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1 and o3-mini).

Provides a critical scientific finding showing that synthetic RSD benchmarks significantly overestimate model performance, exposing severe limitations of current models on real-world document-level cross-lingual alignment.
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement (Spearman correlation between 43.61 and 65.09) is relatively low, reflecting the highly subjective and complex nature of token-level semantic difference annotation.
Limited language diversity: the dataset is English-centric and restricted to high-resource, typologically similar Western European languages using the Latin script.

The absolute performance of all evaluated models on SwissGov-RSD remains extremely low (Spearman correlations under 26), meaning the paper exposes a major challenge but is unable to provide or demonstrate a highly effective baseline solution.

strengths: Introduces the first naturalistic, document-level, cross-lingual dataset (SwissGov-RSD) for token-level semantic difference recognition, filling a significant gap in existing benchmarks which are mostly synthetic or sentence-level.

The annotation process is highly rigorous, employing computational linguistics students who were fairly compensated, utilizing a multi-phase workflow (trial and main phases), and providing transparent analyses of inter-annotator agreement and subjective discrepancies.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation comparing a wide variety of state-of-the-art models, including unsupervised encoders, few-shot LLMs, and models fine-tuned with LLM-based label projection.

Presents important and sobering findings on the massive generalization gap between synthetic and real-world evaluation settings, revealing that high performance on synthetic benchmarks does not translate to naturalistic documents.
weaknesses: The dataset size is relatively small (224 document pairs per language pair), although this is understandable given the high cost and complexity of fine-grained document-level annotation.
Limited language diversity, focusing exclusively on high-resource European languages written in the Latin script (English, German, French, and Italian).

The absolute performance of all baseline models on the new dataset is extremely low (Spearman correlation < 26%), which, while highlighting the difficulty of the task, leaves the path forward for system improvement highly open-ended.
The inter-annotator agreement is relatively low, which is common for fine-grained token-level span tasks but indicates a high level of subjectivity in what constitutes a semantic difference.

strengths: Introduces SwissGov-RSD, the first naturalistic, document-level, cross-lingual dataset for token-level recognition of semantic differences, addressing a major gap in the literature where only synthetic benchmarks existed.
The annotation process is highly rigorous, involving trained annotators, detailed guidelines, fair compensation, and thorough inter-annotator agreement analysis.

Provides a comprehensive and diverse benchmark of state-of-the-art models, including various multilingual encoder models and large language models (LLMs) in multiple settings (unsupervised, few-shot, fine-tuned).
Reveals a critical and insightful performance gap: models that achieve high performance on synthetic datasets fail to generalize to realistic, naturally occurring document-level semantic differences.
weaknesses: The dataset size is relatively small (224 document pairs), which limits its utility for direct supervised training/fine-tuning, making it primarily an evaluation benchmark.

The scope of the languages is limited to English paired with three closely related European languages (German, French, and Italian), leaving the performance on typologically diverse or low-resource languages unexplored.
